question: How did long-term net debt transfers to LMICs change in 2025?
answer: In 2025, long-term net debt transfers to LMICs improved, turning positive after three consecutive years of negative volumes [B-idr2026-p046-c000]. These transfers reversed from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion in 2025 [B-idr2026-p046-c000]. This improvement was driven by a 17.3 percent rise in new gross financing combined with a 2.3 percent increase in debt service payments [B-idr2026-p046-c001]. When China is excluded, the reversal was even more pronounced, moving from an outflow of $48.5 billion to an inflow of $200.5 billion [B-idr2026-p046-c001].

This change is even more pronounced when China is excluded. Net transfers on long-term debt to LMICs excluding China reversed from an outflow of $48.5 billion to an inflow of $200.5 billion. LMICs’ long-term net debt transfers (disbursement minus total debt service payments) turned positive in 2025 after three consecutive years of negative volumes. Negative net transfers were recorded since 2022, during the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, indicating that LMICs’ new disbursements were lower than what they paid in interest and principal payments to service their debt obligations. In 2025, net debt transfers on long-term debt turned positive, reversing from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion (figure 1.7). The improvement was due to net transfers to PPG borrowers, which increased more than sevenfold to $49.9 billion, after turning slightly positive in 2024 to $6.6 billion. Conversely, net debt transfers to PNG borrowers continued to remain negative in 2025, albeit at an improving pace. Net transfers to PNG borrowers remained negative for the fourth consecutive year but improved considerably, from an outflow of $125.0 billion in 2024 to an outflow of $4.5 billion in 2025.

For LMICs excluding China, bondholders provided $70.1 billion more than they received in 2025, after recording five years of outflows from LMICs; commercial banks and other private creditors provided $24.1 billion more in 2025, after recording four years of outflows (figure 1.8).

This behavior is even more evident at the creditor composition level. In 2025, multilateral institutions continued to provide positive support, a trend that has continued since 2007. Net transfers from these institutions increased 36.4 percent in 2025, rebounding from the downward trend recorded since 2022, following the COVID-19 extraordinary financing. During 2025, multilateral institutions provided $21.0 billion more in financing than they received in principal and interest payments. This increase was led by the European Union’s unprecedented support to Ukraine, with the organization providing $32.6 billion more to LMICs than it received in 2025. The World Bank Group was the second-largest provider of net transfers to LMICs during the year, delivering $3.5 billion more than it received. External shocks have compounded preexisting fiscal pressures and increased debt vulnerabilities in LMICs. These countries require substantial investment to raise productivity, create jobs, and advance broader development objectives. Financing these needs depends on mobilizing domestic resources, attracting domestic and foreign private capital, and, where necessary, borrowing through public channels. In this context, part of the increase in public debt reflects efforts to finance infrastructure, human capital, and other investments that can support long-term growth. question: In the chapter on debt transparency (chapter 3), how many countries and loan records does the DRS currently cover?
answer: The Debtor Reporting System (DRS) currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more than 50,000 active loan records [B-idr2026-p121-c002].

The modernization and expansion of the DRS serves as an important anchor for structuring the capacity-building program in debt data management. It currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more than 50,000 active loan records, with approximately 2,500–3,000 new loans reported each year. Maintaining a system of this scale and ensuring the integrity of the data require sustained investment in national reporting capacity. Practical training sessions are not limited to familiarizing debt managers with the new and very different DRS reporting structure. They include equally, if not more, important training in how to implement international statistical standards to categorize and compile debt data. In this context, the overarching goal is to also transmit the skills required to determine if data are complete, internally consistent, appropriately classified, and aligned with international statistical standards. Workshops provide hands-on experience and test runs of the revised classifications and reporting requirements, and explain the links between DRS concepts and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014).

Box 2.2 Strengthening the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries
The 2026 review of the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group updates how the organizations assess sovereign debt risk and sustainability amid rising domestic borrowing, diversified creditor bases, and growing liquidity pressures. The revisions aim to strengthen early warning capacity and policy relevance while preserving the framework’s role in guiding borrowing and lending decisions. Key reforms include the following:

• A revamped risk architecture distinguishing more clearly between external debt stress, overall public debt stress, and unsustainability

• The introduction of new models for the risk of overall public debt stress and public debt unsustainability, together with an updated model for the risk of external public debt stress

Debt distress risks have eased from the deterioration observed over the past decade, particularly following the COVID-19 shock, but they remain elevated. As informed by the World Bank–International Monetary Fund Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries (LIC-DSF), the number of IDA LIC-DSF countries with unsustainable external public debt or rated as being in debt distress remains limited (at end-December 2025): out of 68 IDA LIC-DSF countries, only 11 are in debt distress or have unsustainable public debt. The share of IDA LIC-DSF countries assessed as being at high risk of external debt distress declined from a peak of 46 percent in 2021 to 35 percent in 2025. Most emerging markets remain at low or moderate risk of overall sovereign stress, although vulnerabilities remain uneven, and debt levels are generally above prepandemic levels.

More recently, upgrades have reflected improved macro-fiscal conditions and, in a few cases, the completion of debt restructuring. The LIC-DSF framework underpinning these assessments has undergone a comprehensive review by the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund, with that review approved by their respective Executive Boards in September 2026. Efforts to enhance the debt restructuring architecture continued in 2025 primarily through reforms to the G-20 Common Framework, facilitated by the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. Since its creation in 2020, the G-20 Common Framework has served as the coordinating mechanism for the provision of comprehensive debt restructuring for IDA-eligible countries. It brings together all G-20 bilateral creditors and coordinates with private creditor groups to provide a debt treatment, tailored to each borrower’s debt structure, to restore medium-term debt sustainability. A key area of progress in 2025 was the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable endorsement of early publication by the debtor of the key debt restructuring parameters, namely (a) the net present value reduction; (b) the reduction in debt service over the IMF program period; and (c) the change in the duration of treated claims.
